items.title: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
items.original_title: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
items.summary: A Taiwan Coast Guard patrol vessel moves in Keelung, as China conducts "Justice Mission 2025" military drills around Taiwan, in Keelung, Taiwan, December 30, 2025. REUTERS/Ann Wang TAIPEI, Nov 1 (Reuters) – China’s Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch. China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Taiwan’s Coast Guard said China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality.” “Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added. China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said separately. Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added.

Portchain will operate as an independent company under StormGeo for the next few years and will later be fully integrated into StormGeo’s portfolio. Existing Portchain customers will see no disruption to their service, and the combined offering will be available through StormGeo.

items.title: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight?
items.original_title: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight?
items.summary: In September we borrowed a Led Zeppelin title to describe China’s crude stockpile, a levee holding backthe import shortfall created by the closure of Hormuz. One month on, the wateris still falling, Gulf crude has rambled on around the Strait, and the questionis what it will cost to rebuild. China’s customs crudeimports were 9.03 mbpd in September, broadly flat on August, while refineryruns climbed to 13.99 mbpd, the highest since March. The TD3C premium, in turn, priced the difficulty of leaving the Gulf. Our numbers show who paid that premium: cargoes loaded inside the Strait, on TD3C, and buyers avoided those wherever they could. Crude prices set how much it bought: Brent rose from US$ 72.48 before the war to an intraday high of about US$ 126 on 30 April, and Chinese buying only recovered once it fell below US$ 80 in the summer. September showed the first sustained sign of demand pulling on that system, as freight for VLCCs loading in the Gulf of Oman (TD34) tripled m-o-m, faster than TD3C inside the Strait. The number of VLCCs ballasting towards West Africa, Brazil and the US Gulf fell from about 85 a week in early September to 50 to 54 since mid-October, while transfers off Oman ran at their limits.

items.title: Equinor’s US offshore wind project faces fresh schedule setback
items.original_title: Equinor’s US offshore wind project faces fresh schedule setback
items.summary: Norwegian energy major Equinor has pushed back first power from its $7.5bn Empire Wind offshore wind project in the US to the first half of 2027 over delays with US-built vessels needed for turbine installation. The company disclosed the revised schedule during its third-quarter results presentation, with chief financial officer Torgrim Reitan confirming that the 810MW development off New York is approximately 80% complete. Most of the remaining work involves installing the project’s 54 Vestas 15MW turbines, a campaign now expected to begin early next year, several months later than originally planned. The Maersk Viridis arrived off Mississippi in August for testing and preparations, but delays affecting the feeder vessels have disrupted the offshore installation schedule. Equinor said the revised timetable would not change the project’s overall capital expenditure, estimated at approximately $7.5bn, although some spending would shift into 2027. The company also expects to retain approximately $2.5bn in US investment tax credits, with $2bn expected to be monetised in 2027 and the remainder in 2028. Empire Wind has already completed installation of all 54 turbine foundations, while its offshore substation and offshore cable works are also finished. The project has faced repeated regulatory challenges, including two federal stop-work orders issued by the Trump administration in 2025.

items.title: Shifts in cement trade help support the Supramax market
items.original_title: Shifts in cement trade help support the Supramax market
items.summary: China’s property slump has turned Asia’s cement trade inside out. Its exports are a mix of roughly 60% cement and 40% clinker, and this year the average cargo looks set to travel about three times as far as it did in 2019. These are Supramax-sized parcels on some of the longest routes in the trade, and the new 50% tariff on Canadian cement may stretch them further. They are shipping about a quarter more cement than in 2019, but the tonne-miles have doubled. So every million tonnes that moves from the short route to a long one ties up around four more ships for a year, and across the trade the extra distance since 2019 is worth the full-time work of around 110 Supramaxes in 2026. Because the long hauls go on the bigger ships, Supramax tonne-miles in cement from China and Vietnam look set to rise by more than 80% this year, against about a third for Handysizes. Support for the Supramax market So what does it add up to? When a fleet is close to fully employed, small changes in demand can have an outsized effect on rates, so the extra miles look supportive for Supramax earnings through 2026. The support fades in 2027 as hauls shorten, then levels out in 2028.

items.title: Same Trade Lane, Different Footprint: Carrier Emissions Intensity Differs by Up to 35% on Major Container Routes
items.original_title: Same Trade Lane, Different Footprint: Carrier Emissions Intensity Differs by Up to 35% on Major Container Routes
items.summary: The report also shows why absolute emissions are a poor measure of efficiency. On the China/East Asia–Northern Europe trade, the carrier with the lowest emissions intensity, out of the three carriers examined, also recorded the highest average emissions per voyage, highlighting the importance of cargo volumes and vessel utilization when assessing environmental performance. Based on an analysis of 83,817 voyages performed by 6,730 container-carrying vessels, the report examines how actual vessel operations, including sailing patterns, port stays, cargo utilization and vessel deployment, influence maritime emissions performance. On the Northern Europe–North America East Coast trade, port time jumped 52.1% to 2.1 days. On direct China/East Asia–Northern Europe voyages, Evergreen recorded the highest average emissions of the three carriers examined (14,273 tonnes CO₂e), yet achieved the lowest intensity, at 47.4 g CO₂e/TEU-km, about 17% below the trade average of 57.3. At the same time, NeoPanamax and VLCS made up just 7% of voyages but generated 43% of transport work. This approach enables the company to examine performance across vessels, carriers, routes and operational conditions, rather than relying exclusively on published emission factors or aggregate carrier data. While industry, trade and carrier averages help identify trends, shipment-specific execution data and fuel-consumption modeling provide a more granular basis for understanding transportation performance and identifying opportunities to improve efficiency.

items.title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
items.original_title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
items.summary: Whatever the IMO decides in December, a broker will price a dry bulk trip the next morning. The vote changes which line of that fixture carries the carbon, and how much. The framework was approved in April 2025 and its adoption adjourned for a year last October; it was debated again at MEPC 84 in the spring. From 2028 every tonne of fuel burned on international voyages counts, wherever the ship trades, against two targets: a ship pays $100 for each tonne of CO2-equivalent between the direct-compliance line and the base line, and $380 for each tonne above the base line. On the Rotterdam trip, assuming no change to the European rules, that adds roughly €29,000 in 2028, taking the carbon on the fixture to about €96,000, or €1.45 a tonne and 12% of the hire. For the broker, the practical point is less the price of a tonne of carbon than its allocation. If the framework is adopted, every fixture acquires a carbon line, not only those touching Europe, and the charter party has to say who carries it. On a time-charter trip, the BIMCO clauses written for the EU ETS and FuelEU do not by themselves cover an IMO remedial unit.

items.summary: DOHA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday. “In a scenario where you have a closure of the strait, which is the true contingency that we’re looking to have, you’d immediately see a spike in gas price and you’ll be able to generate revenue for QatarEnergy that otherwise wouldn’t be generated,” Kaabi, who is also the minister of state for energy affairs, said of the plan. Kaabi’s remarks reveal for the first time how Qatar, one of the world’s largest LNG producers, plans to offset lost income from the Iran war and protect revenue against future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. QatarEnergy believes it can leverage its fleet of about 200 LNG tankers, the world’s largest, as well as QatarEnergy Trading, which Kaabi said will soon become the world’s largest gas trading platform. The hedge targets a market transformed after Iran responded to a war launched by the US and Israel on February 28 by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG shipments pass.

The complementary activities and distinctive expertise of the two organisations, together with a focus on continuity, provide a solid basis for a shared vision for long-term growth. Founded in 1828, the Tarros Group is now present throughout the Mediterranean, offering door-to-door transport services and coordinating an integrated logistics network. With 751 employees and an established customer base of 2,700, the Group connects Europe with countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea through a network spanning 16 countries and 31 ports, serving markets with a combined population of more than 500 million people. The agreement covers the acquisition of the Tarros Group as a whole, including the activities and assets that make up its integrated service offering. items.summary: Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. announced the delivery and entry into service of an LNG dual-fuel coal carrier constructed as a dedicated vessel for Kansai Electric Power Co., Inc. The vessel is Japan’s first coal carrier equipped with the Wind Challenger, a hard sail wind-assisted propulsion system. This vessel is engaged in transporting coal to Kansai Electric Power’s Maizuru Power Plant and plays an important role in supporting a stable supply of electricity. To reduce its environmental impact, it features a dual-fuel main engine capable of using LNG as its primary fuel, as well as the Wind Challenger, a wind-assisted propulsion system jointly developed by MOL and Oshima Shipbuilding. Furthermore, the combined effect of the LNG dual-fuel main engine and the Wind Challenger wind-assisted propulsion system is expected to reduce CO2 emissions by up to approximately 30%. Under the MOL Group Environmental Vision – BLUE ACTION 2035 Phase 2, which sets out the MOL Group’s medium- to long-term environmental targets, MOL has established the target of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050. To help achieve this target, the group has identified improvement of fuel efficiency as one of its key actions and plans to deploy 25 Wind Challenger-equipped vessels by 2030 and 80 vessels by 2035.

items.title: Shell and Total Post Highest Quarterly Profit Since 2022
items.original_title: Shell and Total Post Highest Quarterly Profit Since 2022
items.summary: LONDON, Oct 29 (Reuters) – Shell and TotalEnergies reported on Thursday sharply higher third-quarter profits and raised share buybacks, as war-driven energy prices and record refining margins helped both beat expectations. Shell raised its quarterly buyback to $5 billion from $3 billion, the second-largest buyback on record, while Total reiterated plans to buy back $2.5 billion of shares in the fourth quarter and said it would buy back another $2.5 billion in the first quarter of 2027. The shareholder distributions offer an insight into how oil majors plan to spend the profits generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which is in its ninth month and has disrupted global energy supplies. Also on Thursday, Austria’s OMV reported its highest quarterly operating profit since 2022. Refining margins nearly quadrupled for both Shell and Total compared with a year ago. They reached $42 a barrel and $33.2 per barrel, respectively, helping to boost earnings to the highest since 2022, when Shell delivered a record $6 billion buyback program. Shell posted third-quarter net profit of $10.81 billion, above analysts’ average estimate of $10.33 billion and almost double the $5.43 billion it earned a year earlier. Total also took a $1.9 billion impairment mainly tied to offshore wind and a South Korean petrochemical stake.

items.original_title: Port of Tauranga raises $31m from second property sale
items.summary: New Zealand’s Port of Tauranga has completed the sale of a South Island logistics property for NZ$57m ($31m), extending a programme of asset disposals aimed at releasing capital for port infrastructure investment. The NZX-listed port operator said it had sold its 15-hectare property at 5 Baltimore Drive in Rolleston, Canterbury, which includes an intermodal freight hub, a 650 m rail spur and an 18,000 sq m warehouse built in 2019. The industrial-zoned site also contains seven hectares of undeveloped land. The transaction follows the company’s sale of its Gateside industrial property in Auckland to Trade Depot in September for NZ$88.7m ($52m at the time). Chief executive Leonard Sampson said the two sites had been identified for disposal following a review of the group’s property portfolio. The company intends to redirect proceeds from non-core assets into infrastructure supporting its main port and freight operations. The port has said it will seek an expedited court hearing. The Rolleston sale is the second completed property disposal under the current programme. Tauranga has not specified how the proceeds will be allocated between individual infrastructure projects.

items.title: US tightens entry rules for ships calling at Somali ports
items.original_title: US tightens entry rules for ships calling at Somali ports
items.summary: The US Coast Guard has imposed additional security conditions on commercial vessels arriving in American waters after calling at Somali ports, adding the East African country to its list of jurisdictions considered to have inadequate port security measures. The restrictions took effect this week, following a determination that Somalia was not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures at its ports. The decision, published in the US Federal Register, brings the number of countries on the Coast Guard’s affected-port list to 24. Under the established Port Security Advisory framework, ships that have visited an affected country among their previous five port calls face additional security and documentation requirements before entering the US. Vessels may also be inspected for compliance, with deficiencies potentially resulting in delays or denial of entry. The new designation adds a compliance obligation for operators trading between East Africa and the US, including vessels calling at Somali ports before proceeding to other destinations. Somalia joins countries including Iran, Yemen, Libya, Sudan and Venezuela on the list. The Coast Guard removed Nigeria from the advisory in August following a reassessment of its port security arrangements. The measure is separate from maritime warnings concerning piracy and attacks on shipping in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.

The EIA’s crude oil inventory report is a crucial indicator for the energy sector, as it provides insights into the balance of supply and demand within the market. A lesser-than-expected decline in inventories often implies that demand for crude oil is not as robust as projected, which can exert downward pressure on oil prices. Comparatively, the previous week’s data showed a much larger decline in crude oil inventories, with a reported figure of -3.060 million barrels. Conversely, a greater-than-expected decline in inventories often points to stronger demand, buoying prices. As market participants digest the latest data, the focus will likely shift to broader economic indicators and geopolitical factors that could further influence supply and demand dynamics in the oil market.

items.original_title: India greenlights $1bn drive to break China’s container manufacturing dominance
items.summary: India has approved a INR100bn ($1.05bn) programme to massively expand domestic shipping container manufacturing, targeting a tenfold increase in annual capacity as New Delhi seeks to challenge China’s near-monopoly over the industry. The country’s cabinet approved the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme yesterday, turning a proposal announced in February’s national budget into a 13-year industrial development programme. The initiative aims to increase India’s annual container manufacturing capacity from approximately 70,000 teu today to 750,000 teu, potentially establishing the country as a significant international supplier of shipping containers. India hopes to erode that dominance through a combination of production subsidies, subsidised financing and investment in manufacturing infrastructure. The programme includes INR88.91bn in financial assistance for containers manufactured to international standards, alongside INR8.59bn in support for financing new factories and expanding existing production facilities. The government is targeting new factories with annual capacity of at least 100,000 teu, while existing manufacturers must expand capacity by at least 25,000 teu to qualify for financing support. Domestic content requirements will progressively increase from 70% to 90%. The programme runs from the 2027-28 financial year through to 2039-40, allowing three years for establishing facilities followed by ten years of production support.

items.title: Where are all the crew needed going to come from?
items.original_title: Where are all the crew needed going to come from?
items.summary: Shipping has never been short of ambition. The orderbook proves it. But increasingly, the industry again needs to ask itself the uncomfortable question: where are all the crew coming from? Today the physical risks are becoming impossible to ignore. My advice is simple: either manage your crew yourself, or go to where professional crew management is genuinely practised and get involved. The crew should feel that they belong to the owner, not merely to a management company. All too often, supposedly dedicated crew are taken from one owner’s pool and deployed to another owner’s vessel(s) when the manager has an urgent requirement — particularly where immediate matrix or tanker-compliance requirements need to be satisfied. There is simply no manager existing today of the scale and with the reserves of quality crew to take over management of say a large fleet of tankers without taking existing crew from other dedicated pools. Because the next generation of ships may be built of steel, composites, software and sophisticated technology, but without the right people on board, they are simply very expensive assets sitting idle in the water or trading dangerously and unsafely.

items.original_title: Los Angeles, Long Beach Ports Identify LNG and Methanol as Leading Alternative Marine Fuels
items.summary: A CMA CGM containerships waits at anchor outside the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach have identified liquefied natural gas (LNG) and methanol as the most viable alternative marine fuels for the near and medium term, with a new study outlining potential demand and the infrastructure needed to support cleaner shipping at the nation’s busiest port complex. The joint Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , conducted as part of the ports’ Green Shipping Corridor initiatives, examined which alternative fuels shipping companies are most likely to adopt, how demand could develop through 2030, and what investments would be needed to support bunkering operations. The study estimates that annual LNG demand at the San Pedro Bay ports could reach between 65,000 and 115,000 metric tons by 2030, while methanol demand could range from 64,000 to 250,000 metric tons, depending on market conditions and the deployment of alternative-fuel vessels. The report also acknowledges that the environmental benefits of alternative marine fuels depend heavily on how they are produced and sourced. In April, the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach renewed their Green and Digital Shipping Corridor agreement with Singapore, with the partners committing to advance alternative-fuel bunkering, demonstration projects and digital connectivity.

items.summary: The global express and parcels market grew 5.8% in 2025, to €577.3bn ($642.6bn), but mounting pricing pressure, shifting trade flows and intensifying competition are creating a growing challenge for carriers seeking to turn higher volumes into profits. The recent Global Express & Parcels 2026 report by Transport Intelligence predicted that the market would reach €609.1bn this year and €760.1bn by 2030, representing compound annual growth of around 5.7%. Asia Pacific, which in 2024 overtook North America as the largest regional market, is forecast to expand at an annual rate of 8% between 2026 and 2030, while North America is expected to grow 4.1%, and Europe by 3.6%, with several major carriers in mature markets experiencing revenue declines. items.title: Cyclone Arnab brings more disruption along India’s eastern coast
items.original_title: Cyclone Arnab brings more disruption along India’s eastern coast
items.summary: Vessel-handling services have been suspended or restricted across several major ports along India’s east coast since Monday, due to Cyclone Arnab warnings. The severe storm made landfall on India’s eastern coastline this morning, bringing huge swells and gale winds across the region, according to reports. One key gateway port that suspended all operations until further notice was Visakhapatnam, a critical feeder port for Maersk’s coverage out of India’s east coast, especially for cargo moving in and out of Kolkata. Kuehne+Nagel told customers: “Potentially impacted container ports include Visakhapatnam , Gangavaram , and Krishnapatnam , all of which have received cyclone or storm warnings as Arnab approaches India’s east coast.” Industry sources in India believe the port suspensions could inevitably cause congestion and delays to freight flow, but the scale will only be known when terminals fully reopen. Several Indian ports had already been experiencing operational pressures due to widespread vessel bunching tied to delayed arrivals from Asian origin ports, and “the cyclone disruption is another blow to the supply chains”, said a Visakhapatnam-based ship agent. Visakhapatnam handled 302,926 teu year-to-date through September, edging down from 308,861 teu year on year, according to data collected by The Loadstar .

items.title: Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system
items.original_title: Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system
items.summary: A Norwegian-led consortium involving shipbuilder Vard and offshore vessel owner Island Offshore is preparing to build and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system, targeting its first vessel deployment in 2031 or 2032. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, will move from engineering studies to physical integration and testing, with a full-scale test facility planned at Stette near Ålesund in 2027. The project will combine Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MW electric Gem microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems. The initial testing phase will use electric heating instead of nuclear fuel to simulate reactor operation, allowing engineers to assess how the propulsion system performs under realistic vessel operating conditions. Tests will examine normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, system stress, emergency responses and interaction with ship crews. The consortium includes Vard Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk. The initiative builds on the NTNU-led NuProShip research programme, which has been examining the feasibility of integrating advanced nuclear reactors into commercial shipping. The latest pilot has received NOK20m ($2m) from the Research Council of Norway, while its initial development stage is expected to cost approximately NOK150m ($15.6m), including partner contributions.

Net income rose to 5.1 billion riyals ($1.4 billion) from 513 million riyals a year earlier, the company said Wednesday in a stock exchange statement. Sales at its oil unit increased by roughly 10 times due to higher rates and chartering levels. Read more: Saudi Bahri: Sidr Vessel Involved in Aug. 31 Incident in Hormuz Bahri, officially called the National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia, has been instrumental in helping state oil producer Aramco to ramp up crude exports via Hormuz. Overall Gulf oil exports have recovered to near pre-war levels as more regional producers send barrels through Hormuz, relying in part on convoys with military protection and sailing with location signals switched off to avoid detection. items.title: Shipping’s $275m lesson in the limits of sanctions screening
items.original_title: Shipping’s $275m lesson in the limits of sanctions screening
items.summary: A sanctions settlement has exposed a fundamental weakness in shipping’s compliance systems. Wolfgang Lehmacher reports. On paper, Adani Enterprises did what compliance manuals demand. In May 2026, Adani agreed to pay $275m to settle OFAC’s case over 35 cargoes from a Dubai trader that OFAC says were Iranian. In February 2024, the trader’s bank stopped payment for one shipment. When the Forced Labour Regulation applies in December 2027, customs will be able to stop banned products at the border, and missing traceability information may count against a company. A permissioned record of where cargo was loaded, what carried it and who handled it would give customs, banks and insurers the evidence they demand. And which parts of the voyage record do we depend on others for, and on what terms? Every voyage leaves a trail at the berth, on the bridge and in the bunker log.

items.title: Iran singles out Sinokor
items.original_title: Iran singles out Sinokor
items.summary: Iran has threatened South Korean tanker giant Sinokor, the world’s dominant VLCC owner, with sweeping action against its fleet from November 1, accusing the company of repeatedly violating Tehran’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) has said Sinokor vessels have committed more transit violations than any other operator over the past three months, claiming enforcement measures have already been taken against at least seven ships. The authority has warned cargo owners, charterers and insurers that all Sinokor-linked vessels will face “legal action” from Sunday, although it has not specified what that might entail. Sinokor has emerged as the dominant tanker player in the Gulf since the conflict began, rapidly expanding its VLCC fleet and capitalising on extraordinary freight rates. According to Bloomberg vessel-tracking analysis, Sinokor-controlled tankers carried approximately 105.6m barrels of crude through Hormuz in September, representing 37% of total volumes. Sinokor is seeking clarification of Iran’s warning. Iran’s navy claimed yesterday that an unidentified tanker caught fire after striking mines east of Hormuz while operating with its tracking equipment switched off. The claim has not been independently verified. The announcement directly challenges US Central Command’s assertion on Sunday that the strait’s main shipping lanes had been cleared of Iranian mines.

items.title: Maritime CEO Forum: Shipping’s wartime boom tests discipline
items.original_title: Maritime CEO Forum: Shipping’s wartime boom tests discipline
items.summary: Shipping may be enjoying one of its strongest booms in decades, but the extraordinary profits generated by geopolitical turmoil are raising difficult questions about risk, investment and what happens when the wars end, delegates at yesterday’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco heard. Opening the event at the Yacht Club de Monaco, Splash editor Sam Chambers asked whether today’s riches were encouraging owners to repeat the mistakes of past cycles. Burak Cetinok, head of research at Arrow, described the rally as unusually broad across freight, vessel values and sale-and-purchase activity. His biggest concern was fresh capacity: Arrow’s analysis suggested that once an orderbook reaches roughly 25% of the existing fleet, earnings have historically tended to fall within 24 to 36 months. By the end of 2029, he said, almost half the fleet would be over 15 years old and a quarter over 20, creating considerable replacement demand. With tanker owners generally carrying much less debt than before the 2008 crash, he argued, the industry was also more resilient. Illustrating the desperation to secure oil supplies, Harfjeld described a refinery customer accepting a voyage 40 days longer, at a 50% higher freight rate, to avoid heightened Red Sea risks. A flattening between spot and forward freight rates would be one sign that the boom was losing momentum.

items.title: Wallenius Wilhelmsen extends car carrier newbuild drive
items.original_title: Wallenius Wilhelmsen extends car carrier newbuild drive
items.summary: Norwegian car carrier giant Wallenius Wilhelmsen has moved to extend its fleet renewal programme, following a $300m capital raise earlier this month to support plans for up to 12 additional LNG dual-fuel vessels. The Oslo-listed group issued a fresh update on its newbuilding programme on Wednesday, three weeks after outlining plans to add four large car carriers for delivery in 2030, with options for another eight ships. Under the earlier proposal, optional vessels would arrive quarterly from 2031 onwards, potentially expanding the company’s overall newbuilding programme to 26 vessels, including options, through 2032. Wallenius Wilhelmsen completed a NOK2.88bn ($300m) private placement on October 6, issuing 17.145m shares at NOK168 each. The proceeds, together with debt financing, were earmarked for its enlarged shipbuilding programme. The expansion builds on the company’s existing Shaper-class newbuilding series at China Merchants Jinling Shipyard in China, where it has contracted 14 vessels. The ships comprise six 9,300 ceu units and eight larger car carriers with nominal capacity of 11,700 ceu. Seven feature LNG dual-fuel propulsion, while the remaining seven use methanol dual-fuel engines. The newbuilding programme is intended to replace ageing tonnage and support the company’s long-term vehicle shipping requirements, with the group operating around 127 vessels across 15 global trade routes.

Splash understands the George Delaportas-controlled outfit has contracted six 64,500 dwt vessels, with deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. Shipbuilding sources said the conventionally fuelled vessels would be based on Xiangyu’s second-generation Elephant design. Meadway has built much of its modern fleet through Japanese shipyards, including Namura and Imabari, as well as Japan’s Tsuneishi group, which operates a shipyard in Zhoushan, China. In September, it welcomed the Elisabetta , a 66,000 dwt TESS66 Aeroline ultramax built at Tsuneishi Zhoushan, following other newbuilding additions earlier in 2026. In January, the company added the 2016-built, 64,507 dwt Good Carry , formerly Diana Shipping’s DSI Drammen , in a deal valued at approximately $26.4m. This was followed by the 2012 Oshima-built ultramax Arabica in February for roughly $19m. Meadway has another 64,000 dwt ultramax under construction at Imabari Shipbuilding in Japan, with delivery scheduled for the second quarter of 2027. The Athens-based company was established by George Delaportas in 2021 following the separation of the family’s shipping interests.

items.title: Venergy breaks into VLCCs with Hengli order
items.original_title: Venergy breaks into VLCCs with Hengli order
items.summary: Greek shipowner Vyron Vasileiadis is taking his rapidly expanding tanker business into the VLCC segment, with Venergy Maritime linked to two firm newbuildings and options for another two at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries. The latest deal involves 306,000 dwt crude carriers, with deliveries reportedly scheduled for the first quarter of 2029, according to Greek shipbuilding sources. The move marks another expansion of Venergy’s newbuilding programme, which has grown at considerable pace since Vasileiadis entered independent shipowning last year. The company initially moved into the sector through the acquisition of three MR2 product tankers, before ordering eight MR2 newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding and six LR2s at China’s New Times Shipbuilding. Venergy has since moved into larger crude carriers, accumulating eight suezmax newbuildings across Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding, Guangzhou Shipyard International and Hengli. The relationship with Hengli began in June with a two-plus-two suezmax contract. Venergy exercised the two options in September, taking its firm series at the Dalian yard to four 158,000 dwt tankers. The latest VLCC agreement would give Venergy another two firm crude tankers and the possibility of adding a further pair. Including its associated OceanV Maritime containership programme, Vasileiadis’ overall newbuilding pipeline could reach 34 vessels if the remaining VLCC options are exercised.

The vessels are intended for a range of subsea construction and offshore energy operations, with an emphasis on operational flexibility and energy efficiency. This confirms an order Siem Industries first disclosed in August, when the company said it had contracted two subsea construction newbuilds at an unnamed Chinese shipyard. At the time, it revealed no further details. Sirius separately announced a design contract that month for two 144.7-m construction support vessels at Fujian Mawei. The naval architect said the design would include two launch-and-recovery systems for remotely operated vehicles and provisions for additional equipment, including a carousel and vertical lay system.
